opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really good question, and honestly it's something I think about a lot. The way I see it, every researcher has a kind of world model, a set of priors about what works and what doesn't, and those priors are built from years of running experiments, reading papers, and getting burned by things that didn't pan out. That's valuable, but it's also dangerous, because the field moves so fast that some of those priors just become stale.

So when a new paradigm shows up, whether it was the shift to scaling, or instruction tuning, or now the whole reasoning and RL-on-top-of-LLMs wave, the first thing I try to do is be honest with myself about whether my skepticism is grounded in evidence or just in comfort. A lot of the time, being skeptical feels smart, because most new ideas don't work. But the ones that do work tend to really change everything, and if your learning rate is too low, you just miss the boat.

What I try to do in practice is crank up the learning rate temporarily. I go and get my hands dirty: run the thing, look at the outputs, talk to the people who believe in it most strongly. There's no substitute for direct contact with the experiments. Reading Twitter threads or abstracts gives you a very noisy gradient. Actually training the model and seeing the loss curves gives you a much cleaner signal.

At the same time, you don't want to overfit to every new trend, because there's a lot of hype and many things are just repackaged old ideas. So I try to separate what is fundamentally new, maybe a new axis of scaling, from what is just a new name. If it's a new axis, I update hard. If it's a rebrand, I update a little and move on.

And the meta-lesson I've learned over the years is that being wrong is fine; staying wrong is the problem. Some of the best researchers I've worked with are the ones who can say, "Okay, I was totally wrong about this, here's my new view," without any ego attached. That ability to update quickly, almost like having a good optimizer for your own beliefs, is probably one of the most underrated skills in this field.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a fun way to frame it. I actually think about this a lot, because I've been on the wrong side of it more than once.

So the honest version is: my learning rate used to be too low. When I was at Google Brain working on architectures, I had a pretty strong prior that the interesting work was in the model itself. Attention variants, efficient transformers, all of that. And then scaling just kind of ran over all of us. The thing that mattered wasn't the clever architecture, it was data and compute and getting the infrastructure right. I remember feeling almost offended by it at first, which in hindsight is a very bad signal. If a result annoys you, that's usually your world model complaining, not the result being wrong.

So now I try to do a few things. One is I separate taste from belief. Taste is the stuff I genuinely enjoy working on, and I don't think you should update that too aggressively, because it's what keeps you productive. Belief is the stuff about what actually works, and that should have a much higher learning rate. When a new paradigm shows up, I ask myself: is this challenging my taste or my belief? If it's just my taste, fine, I can be grumpy about it privately. If it's my belief, I have to actually go run the experiment.

The second thing is I try to be the one who disproves my own position before someone else does. Like with encoder-decoder versus decoder-only, I had strong opinions for a long time, and I eventually just forced myself to look at the evidence cleanly and go, okay, a lot of this doesn't matter at scale, let it go. It's much less painful to update yourself than to be updated by a leaderboard.

And then the third thing, which I think people underrate, is that you don't have to take the whole paradigm. New paradigms come with a lot of noise and hype attached, and the worst outcome is overshooting and becoming a hype person who believes everything. So I try to find the one or two load-bearing claims, test those, and only move my weights there. Learning rate schedules should have warmup, basically. Don't jump straight to the maximum on day one of a new trend.

The honest meta-point is that the field punishes stubbornness more than it punishes being early and wrong. So I'd rather err on the side of updating a bit too fast now, and I say that as someone whose natural setting is definitely the opposite.

astra-6.text:
I think you want a high learning rate for evidence, but a lower learning rate for the story you build around it. When a new result challenges my intuition, I want to understand it quickly: what actually changed, what did they measure, and which assumption of mine does it contradict? But I don’t necessarily want to rewrite my entire world model based on one result.

In research, you develop intuitions because they’ve helped you make progress. The danger is that you become attached to them. So I’d try to make the disagreement concrete. If I think something shouldn’t work and it does, can I run a small experiment that helps me understand why? That’s much more useful than debating whether the whole paradigm is right or wrong.

And the update doesn’t have to be all or nothing. Maybe the result is real, but my explanation for it is wrong. Maybe it works in a regime I hadn’t considered. You want enough stability to pursue an idea through uncertainty, but enough flexibility to recognize when the evidence is telling you to change direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to have a high learning rate for new evidence, but a lower learning rate for the narrative around it. When something new works, I want to understand why it works, what assumptions it breaks, and whether I can reproduce the result. That should change my world model more than how excited everyone is about it.

There’s also a danger in becoming too attached to your own research. You’ve invested years in a particular approach, so you naturally want the next paradigm to be a special case of what you already believed. I think you have to be willing to say, okay, maybe this changes the problem entirely.

But being open-minded doesn’t mean resetting your beliefs every week. I’d rather run a small experiment, build some intuition, and update from that. Have strong convictions about doing the work, and hold the explanations a little more loosely.
